power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report:
This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 38 R code files.
#### Run order
A dependency **cycle** was detected among 8 files (aigfield.R, aiscored.R, catbank.R, essays.R, itemtext.R, linking.R, numeracy.R, openended.R): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:30, File = c("00-author.Rmd", "01-measurement.Rmd", 
"02-irt-models.Rmd", "03-estimation.Rmd", "04-dimensionality.Rmd", 
"05-fit.Rmd", "06-information.Rmd", "07-scoring.Rmd", "08-polytomous.Rmd", 
"09-dif.Rmd", "10-linking.Rmd", "11-banks-cat.Rmd", "12-reporting.Rmd",

"none", "none", "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -30L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **1 data path was built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `hexaco items.csv`, `hexaco responses.csv`.
#### Execution
**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 38 scripts: 13 ran without error, 19 errored, 0 timed out, 6 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: Item response theory (IRT) is the statistical foundation of most modern tests: It links the responses people give to test items with the latent trait the test is meant to measure, and it underpins item banking, test assembly, computerized adaptive testing, score linking and fairness analyses (de Ayala, 2022; Embretson & Reise, 2000; Lord, 1980).
text.formatted: Item response theory (IRT) is the statistical foundation of most modern tests: It links the responses people give to test items with the latent trait the test is meant to measure, and it underpins item banking, test assembly, computerized adaptive testing, score linking and fairness analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(de Ayala, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Embretson & Reise, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Lord, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: The R environment (R Core Team, 2026) offers many IRT packages, and among them mirt (Chalmers, 2012) stands out for the breadth of models and estimation methods it supports.
text.formatted: The R environment (R Core Team, 2026) offers many IRT packages, and among them mirt <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chalmers, 2012)</ref> stands out for the breadth of models and estimation methods it supports.

text.text: Its power comes with a cost, however: Choosing, checking, interpreting and reporting a model in mirt requires fluency in both R and psychometrics. mirtverse (Bulut, 2026b) is an R package that sits on top of mirt and makes it usable by a wider audience.
It turns fitted mirt models into tidy tables, publication-ready ggplot2 graphics (Wickham, 2016), plain-language interpretations, item health cards, one-file HTML reports and shareable dashboards.
A point-and-click Shiny workbench runs the same functions and writes the R code for every step.

Beyond the usual IRT toolkit, mirtverse adds a generative AI layer that writes analysis scripts from a plain-language request, drafts and verifies test items, trains and audits automated scorers for open-ended responses, and predicts item difficulty from item text.
Every AI feature sits behind a psychometric check, so a language model can speed up the work but cannot quietly lower its standards.
The package is accompanied by an open textbook (Bulut, 2026a), ten interactive teaching labs and an instructor toolkit.
This paper reviews the theory that mirtverse builds on, the current landscape of IRT software in R, the reasons for building on mirt, and the design of mirtverse, including its AI capabilities.
IRT is taught in graduate programs in education, psychology and the health sciences, and it is used every day by testing organizations, credentialing bodies and researchers who build questionnaires.
Yet the people who need IRT results are often not the people who can produce them.
Three gaps stand out.
The skills gap.
Fitting a model is one line of code in most packages, but the analysis around it is not:

Comparing candidate models, checking dimensionality, local independence and item fit, interpreting parameters, and reporting the results in a form that a committee, a content team or a policy maker can use.
Students and practitioners who are new to R often stall at this stage, and many fall back on commercial pointand-click programs that hide the analysis behind menus.
The reporting gap.
Psychometric output is designed for psychometricians.
Item reviewers, teachers and test sponsors need summaries, flags and figures rather than parameter tables, and assembling those by hand is slow and error-prone.
The AI gap.
Large language models (LLMs) and machine learning now generate items, score essays and estimate item properties (Bulut et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Large language models (LLMs) and machine learning now generate items, score essays and estimate item properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bulut et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hao et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Most psychometricians, however, have no practical way to try these methods within their usual workflow, and the methods themselves need the same validity and fairness evidence as any other part of a test (American Educational Research Association et al.,  2014;Kane, 2013; Williamson et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Most psychometricians, however, have no practical way to try these methods within their usual workflow, and the methods themselves need the same validity and fairness evidence as any other part of a test (American Educational Research Association et al.,  2014;<ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Kane, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Williamson et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: mirtverse addresses all three gaps without replacing the estimation engine that psychometricians already trust.
Every mirtverse result is computed from an ordinary mirt model object, so analyses remain reproducible, citable and open to inspection by anyone who knows mirt.
IRT models the probability of a response as a function of a person's position on a latent trait, 𝜃, and the characteristics of the item.

For a dichotomously scored item 𝑗, the three-parameter logistic (3PL) model (Birnbaum, 1968) is where 𝑏 𝑗 is the item's difficulty, 𝑎 𝑗 its discrimination and 𝑐 𝑗 a lower asymptote that allows for guessing.
text.formatted: For a dichotomously scored item 𝑗, the three-parameter logistic (3PL) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Birnbaum, 1968)</ref> is where 𝑏 𝑗 is the item's difficulty, 𝑎 𝑗 its discrimination and 𝑐 𝑗 a lower asymptote that allows for guessing.

text.text: Fixing 𝑐 𝑗 = 0 gives the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model, and also constraining all 𝑎 𝑗 to be equal gives the Rasch model (Rasch, 1960), whose sufficient statistics and specific objectivity have made it popular in educational assessment and health outcomes measurement.
text.formatted: Fixing 𝑐 𝑗 = 0 gives the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model, and also constraining all 𝑎 𝑗 to be equal gives the Rasch model <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rasch, 1960)</ref>, whose sufficient statistics and specific objectivity have made it popular in educational assessment and health outcomes measurement.

text.text: For items scored in more than two ordered categories, the graded response model (Samejima, 1969), the partial credit model (Masters, 1982) and the generalized partial credit model (Muraki, 1992) extend the same logic to category response functions.
text.formatted: For items scored in more than two ordered categories, the graded response model <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Samejima, 1969)</ref>, the partial credit model <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Masters, 1982)</ref> and the generalized partial credit model <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Muraki, 1992)</ref> extend the same logic to category response functions.

text.text: Three properties make IRT more useful than classical test theory for many practical problems (Embretson & Reise, 2000; Hambleton et al., 1991).
text.formatted: Three properties make IRT more useful than classical test theory for many practical problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Embretson & Reise, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hambleton et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: First, item and person parameters are placed on a common scale, which supports item banking, linking and equating across test forms (Kolen & Brennan, 2014).
text.formatted: First, item and person parameters are placed on a common scale, which supports item banking, linking and equating across test forms <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kolen & Brennan, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the item information function, 𝐼 𝑗 (𝜃), shows how precisely each item measures at each trait level, and the test information 𝐼(𝜃) = ∑ 𝑗 𝐼 𝑗 (𝜃) gives a conditional standard error, 𝑆𝐸( θ) = 1/√𝐼(𝜃), rather than a single reliability coefficient for everyone.
This is what makes computerized adaptive testing possible (Wainer et al., 2000).
text.formatted: This is what makes computerized adaptive testing possible <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Wainer et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Third, the model makes testable predictions, so its assumptions can and should be checked.

Item parameters are usually estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm (Bock & Aitkin, 1981), which integrates the latent trait out of the likelihood; stochastic algorithms such as the Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro (MH-RM) algorithm (Cai, 2010) make high-dimensional and mixedeffects models feasible (Chalmers, 2015).
text.formatted: Item parameters are usually estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bock & Aitkin, 1981)</ref>, which integrates the latent trait out of the likelihood; stochastic algorithms such as the Metropolis-Hastings Robbins-Monro (MH-RM) algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cai, 2010)</ref> make high-dimensional and mixedeffects models feasible <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chalmers, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Once a model is fitted, a defensible analysis checks overall fit, for example with the limited-information 𝑀 2 statistic and its RMSEA (Maydeu-Olivares & Joe, 2006); item fit, for example with the 𝑆-𝑋 2 statistic (Orlando & Thissen, 2000); local dependence, for example with Yen's 𝑄 3 (Yen, 1984); and differential item functioning (DIF) between groups of test takers (Holland & Wainer, 1993).
text.formatted: Once a model is fitted, a defensible analysis checks overall fit, for example with the limited-information 𝑀 2 statistic and its RMSEA <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Maydeu-Olivares & Joe, 2006)</ref>; item fit, for example with the 𝑆-𝑋 2 statistic <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Orlando & Thissen, 2000)</ref>; local dependence, for example with Yen's 𝑄 3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Yen, 1984)</ref>; and differential item functioning (DIF) between groups of test takers <ref type="bibr">(Holland & Wainer, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Persons are then scored, typically by expected a posteriori (EAP) or maximum likelihood estimation, with standard errors.
Two extensions matter for what follows.
Explanatory IRT models (De Boeck & Wilson, 2004) replace or explain item and person parameters with covariates.
text.formatted: Explanatory IRT models <ref type="bibr">(De Boeck & Wilson, 2004</ref>) replace or explain item and person parameters with covariates.

text.text: The linear logistic test model (Fischer, 1973), for instance, expresses item difficulty as a weighted sum of item features, which connects IRT to the modern task of predicting item difficulty from item text.
text.formatted: The linear logistic test model <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fischer, 1973)</ref>, for instance, expresses item difficulty as a weighted sum of item features, which connects IRT to the modern task of predicting item difficulty from item text.

text.text: And joint models for responses and response times (van der Linden, 2007) use the time each person spends on each item as a second source of information about speed, effort and test-taking behaviour.
R has become one of the main platforms for IRT, and several reviews compare the available packages (Choi & Asilkalkan, 2019).
text.formatted: R has become one of the main platforms for IRT, and several reviews compare the available packages <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Choi & Asilkalkan, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Table 1 summarises widely used packages and their focus.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> summarises widely used packages and their focus.

text.text: These packages are strong at estimation, and some, such as ShinyItemAnalysis, lower the barrier to entry with a graphical interface.

What remains largely missing is a layer that takes a fitted model from a general-purpose engine and carries it through the steps that come after estimation: Choosing among models with a stated reason, checking it, explaining it in plain language, reporting it to non-specialists, and connecting it to the operational and AI-assisted tasks that modern testing programs face.
Commercial programs offer parts of this, but they are closed, costly and hard to reproduce.
mirtverse could have wrapped any estimation engine.
It builds on mirt for four reasons.

First, breadth: mirt fits unidimensional and multidimensional models, bifactor and two-tier structures, multiple-group and mixed-effects models, and item types from the Rasch model to the nominal response model, so one interface serves classroom examples and operational programs alike (Chalmers, 2012 (Chalmers, , 2015)).
text.formatted: First, breadth: mirt fits unidimensional and multidimensional models, bifactor and two-tier structures, multiple-group and mixed-effects models, and item types from the Rasch model to the nominal response model, so one interface serves classroom examples and operational programs alike <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Chalmers, 2012</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chalmers, , 2015))</ref>.

text.text: Second, estimation choices: EM, quasi-Monte Carlo EM and MH-RM cover both small and high-dimensional problems (Cai, 2010).
text.formatted: Second, estimation choices: EM, quasi-Monte Carlo EM and MH-RM cover both small and high-dimensional problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Cai, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Third, diagnostics: 𝑀 2 and its fit indices, 𝑆-𝑋 2 item fit, residual-based local dependence statistics, DIF and differential test functioning, several scoring methods and plausible values are already built in.
Fourth, an ecosystem: mirtCAT (Chalmers, 2016) extends mirt to adaptive testing, and mirt is actively maintained and widely cited.
text.formatted: Fourth, an ecosystem: mirtCAT <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chalmers, 2016)</ref> extends mirt to adaptive testing, and mirt is actively maintained and widely cited.

text.text: By keeping mirt's model objects as the single source of truth, mirtverse can add convenience without introducing a second set of estimates that could disagree with the first.
mirtverse is organised in layers around the mirt model object (Figure 1).
text.formatted: mirtverse is organised in layers around the mirt model object (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Each layer can be used on its own, and higher layers only call the lower ones.

Choosing and explaining a model. select_model() fits a set of candidate models to the same data, ranks them by an information criterion, runs likelihood-ratio tests between nested models, reports absolute fit, and states the recommendation and its reasons in plain language, including where the criteria disagree. interpret() writes a structured plain-language summary of overall fit, reliability, targeting, flagged items and local dependence.

item_table() and item_card() collect each item's statistics, fit and flags, and render a one-page "health card" with a green, amber or red rating for item review meetings. cite_methods() drafts the Methods paragraph of a thesis or article in APA style, with every number taken from the fitted model and a matching reference list.

Sharing. mv_report() writes a single self-contained HTML report, and mv_dashboard() an interactive dashboard for readers who never open R (Figure 2). launch_workbench() opens a Shiny application with eight tabs (data, exploration, model choice, results, scores, response times, report and code, and an operational pipeline).
text.formatted: Sharing. mv_report() writes a single self-contained HTML report, and mv_dashboard() an interactive dashboard for readers who never open R (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>). launch_workbench() opens a Shiny application with eight tabs (data, exploration, model choice, results, scores, response times, report and code, and an operational pipeline).

text.text: Every action in the workbench is recorded as R code that the user can download and rerun, so the point-and-click route leads into R rather than away from it.
Figure 2.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>.

text.text: Outputs produced by mirtverse: A results dashboard, an item health card, a Wright map and a DIF plot.

Beyond estimation. fit_rt() estimates a hierarchical model for responses and response times (van der Linden, 2007) and flags rapid guessing. mirtify() translates code written for ltm, eRm, TAM or irtQ into the equivalent mirt code, which lowers the cost of moving existing analyses.
The mv_pipeline() family links these functions into a full assessment pipeline, described below.
Design trade-offs.
Three decisions shape the package.
First, mirtverse never re-estimates what mirt estimates: It reads mirt objects and calls mirt functions, which keeps results identical to mirt and lets mirtverse benefit from every mirt improvement.

Where an established method was missing or outdated in R, it was implemented in base R and compared with existing implementations: The response-time model was checked against LNIRT, and classification accuracy and consistency against cacIRT.
Second, dependencies are kept light.
Machine learning models in the AI layer, such as ridge and lasso regression and random forests, are implemented in base R, and heavier engines such as eatATA for automated test assembly are optional.

Third, interpretation rules are explicit and adjustable: The thresholds behind every flag and plain-language verdict live in one place, mv_rules(), so users can see and change them rather than trust a black box.
The AI layer follows one principle: Every AI feature sits behind a psychometric check.
Language models are reached through the ellmer package (Wickham et al., 2026), so users can choose Claude, an OpenAI model or a local model through Ollama when data must stay on their own computer.
text.formatted: Language models are reached through the ellmer package <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Wickham et al., 2026)</ref>, so users can choose Claude, an OpenAI model or a local model through Ollama when data must stay on their own computer.

text.text: A replay mode answers requests from recorded responses, so every AI example runs in class without an API key or an internet connection.
Analysis scripts from a plain-language request. mv_ask() turns a request such as "fit a 2PL, check DIF by gender and make a report" into a structured analysis plan.
The plan fills tested code templates rather than asking the model to write free-form code, and the script is shown before anything runs.
Only metadata, such as column names, is sent to the model, and these can be anonymised; without a model, an offline keyword parser fills the same plan.

Item generation and verification. generate_items() drafts multiple-choice items with keys and rationales, or open-ended items with scoring rubrics, from a test blueprint. verify_items() then asks a second, independent model call to answer each item without seeing the key, and flags disagreements, weak distractors and nearduplicates before any person reviews the items.

For template-based automatic item generation (Gierl & Haladyna, 2013), item_model() and generate_isomorphs() create item families from an item model, and calibrate_families() estimates how much item parameters vary within each family.
text.formatted: For template-based automatic item generation <ref type="bibr">(Gierl & Haladyna, 2013)</ref>, item_model() and generate_isomorphs() create item families from an item model, and calibrate_families() estimates how much item parameters vary within each family.

text.text: Automated scoring with an agreement gate. train_scorer() fits a transparent scoring engine (ridge regression on words and word pairs) to human-scored responses and reports cross-validated accuracy, and score_open() scores new responses with that engine or with an LLM and a rubric. agreement_report() then judges the machine scores the way the measurement literature recommends (Williamson et al., 2012): Quadratic weighted kappa against humans and against the human-human benchmark, standardized mean differences overall and within each subgroup, and proportional reduction in mean squared error.
text.formatted: Automated scoring with an agreement gate. train_scorer() fits a transparent scoring engine (ridge regression on words and word pairs) to human-scored responses and reports cross-validated accuracy, and score_open() scores new responses with that engine or with an LLM and a rubric. agreement_report() then judges the machine scores the way the measurement literature recommends <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Williamson et al., 2012)</ref>: Quadratic weighted kappa against humans and against the human-human benchmark, standardized mean differences overall and within each subgroup, and proportional reduction in mean squared error.

text.text: Machine scores are not used until they pass.
ai_audit() and validity_argument() assemble the evidence into a Kane-style validity argument (Kane, 2013) for the technical report.
text.formatted: ai_audit() and validity_argument() assemble the evidence into a Kane-style validity argument <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Kane, 2013)</ref> for the technical report.

text.text: Item text and difficulty. item_features() computes features of the item text, such as length, readability, numerical content and similarity to other items, which also exposes near-duplicate items. predict_difficulty() compares a two-step linear logistic test model (Fischer, 1973) with lasso and random forest models under crossvalidation, reports how close any model can get given the estimation error in the item parameters, and warns when a feature appears to have been computed from the field-test data itself.

text.text: An experimental simulate_llm_respondents() lets researchers compare LLM-simulated answers with real response data, and it is labelled experimental throughout because the validity of synthetic respondents is still an open research question.
The examples in this section use mirtverse as an extension of mirt for the analyses psychometricians already run.
Every model is an ordinary mirt model, so anything mirt can do with it still works.
The following code compares the Rasch and 2PL models for 32 scored multiple-choice items answered by 600 students (the SAT12 data in mirt), explains the choice, and drafts the Methods paragraph:
The certexam data in mirtverse hold a 32-item certification exam taken by 1,200 candidates in English or French.
dif() runs likelihood-ratio DIF tests with mirt with a Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment and effect sizes for every item, and interpret() explains the result:
The summary separates a real difference in ability between the groups from DIF, names the items, says which group each one favours and how much, and points to the plot that shows the crossing curves.
It ends with the caution a psychometrician would give a student: A flagged item goes to content experts before it is removed.
The examples in this section use the AI layer.
Each one runs without an API key: Item models and scoring engines are fitted in R, and the language model calls answer from recorded responses in replay mode.

text.text: Analysis scripts from plain-language requests mv_ask() turns a request in everyday language into an analysis plan, fills the plan from tested code templates, and shows the R script before anything runs.
The examples go from simple to more complex.
The simplest request names only a model, and the offline keyword parser is enough: A longer request adds item fit and a DIF analysis by a grouping column.
The plan lists every assumption it made, and the script uses only mirt and mirtverse functions:
A request phrased as a researcher would say it goes to a language model.
The model sees only a description of the columns, never the responses, and returns the same structured plan.

text.text: When a request leaves out something the analysis needs, mv_ask() asks instead of guessing.
"Check DIF" on data with no column named in the request stops with the question "Which column holds the groups to compare for DIF?".
Because the code always comes from the same templates, the script that runs does not depend on whether a language model or the keyword parser read the request.

An item model is a template whose numbers vary while the task stays the same. generate_isomorphs() fills it with values that meet the constraints and drops any item whose options are not all different:
Each distractor comes from a named misconception, so an error in the model is caught for all of its items at once.
After a field test, calibrate_families() checks whether the items of each family are equally difficult.
In the aigfield data, 60 items from six item models were given to 1,000 students:
Here calibrated holds each item's difficulty (b) and its standard error from a 2PL model fitted with mirt.
Four families are isomorphic, so a new item from them can be used with its family's mean difficulty in place of a field test of several hundred students (field_n).
Two are not: Some subtraction (SUB) items need regrouping, which makes them harder, and two triangle (TRI) items have two identical options.
For items written by a language model rather than a template, generate_items() drafts items from a blueprint and verify_items() has a second model call answer each one without the key.

text.text: A scoring engine is trained on 400 essays that two human raters have scored, and its cross-validated scores are checked against the raters:
Overall, the engine agrees with the raters better than the raters agree with each other.
Within the group of English language learners, however, its scores are systematically too low, and the report says so (Figure 3).
text.formatted: Within the group of English language learners, however, its scores are systematically too low, and the report says so (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">3</ref>).

text.text: A scorer judged only on overall agreement would have passed; a psychometric check catches the problem before any score is reported.
A scoring engine is one AI component among several, and a testing program needs one place to check them all before results are used. ai_audit() runs these checks in a single call.
In the aiscored data, an engine scores four constructed-response items (CR1 to CR4) on a 20-item test over two years, and a validity sample of responses was also scored by two human raters:
Each flag names the item, the evidence and what to do next.

Two problems block the use of the scores: On CR2, the engine gives English language learners lower scores than fluent students whose responses the human raters scored the same, the comparison that separates bias in the engine from real group differences (Johnson et al., e1 <-essays[essays$prompt == "E1", ] s <-train_scorer(e1) a <-agreement_report(s$cv$machine, e1$human1, e1$human2, group = e1$group) a #> group n qwk qwk_human smd verdict #> All 400 0.89 0.83 -0.03 meets #> Fluent 300 0.91 0.82 -0.00 meets #> ELL 100 0.81 0.86 -0.12 machine too low d26 <-aiscored[aiscored$year == 2026, ] audit <-ai_audit(aiscored_cr, human2 = "human2", group = "group", item = "item", period = "year", responses = d26[, -(1:3)], person_group = d26$group) audit #> AI audit: 7 checks, 8 flags (2 block, 5 review) #> check tested flagged status #> human agreement 4 1 REVIEW #> machine agreement 4 1 REVIEW #> overall bias 4 0 ok #> subgroup agreement 8 2 REVIEW #> differential scoring 4 1 BLOCK #> drift 4 1 BLOCK #> DIF 20 2 REVIEW #> #> Flags: #> [BLOCK] differential scoring, CR2, ELL: gap -0.31 SD, SE 0.05.

The audit also shows that the human raters disagree on CR4, so the rubric, not the engine, needs attention first. validity_argument(audit) turns these results into the validity section of the technical report.
Before a field test, a language model can answer items in the role of described test takers.
simulate_llm_respondents() collects these answers and compare_synthetic() sets them beside real data.
Here 12 personas answer 12 numeracy items whose field-test difficulties are known:
The comparison is the point of the example.

Synthetic respondents are marked as experimental in mirtverse, and the package says plainly what they cannot do: They are useful for finding unclear items or planning a study, not for estimating item parameters or replacing a field test.
The examples above are single analyses.
A testing program needs all of them, in order, with a record of every decision.

The mv_pipeline() family brings the traditional and the AI-based functions together in one object that carries a test through thirteen stages, from the blueprint to the monitoring of the item bank after each administration (Figure 4).
text.formatted: The mv_pipeline() family brings the traditional and the AI-based functions together in one object that carries a test through thirteen stages, from the blueprint to the monitoring of the item bank after each administration (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: The stages fall into four phases:
A blueprint records what the test measures, how its scores will be used and how many items each content cell needs.
Items are drafted by a language model or written by people, the keys of generated items are checked by a second model call, and a review packet goes to content and sensitivity reviewers.
A field-test design spreads the items over forms with shared anchors and simulates how well the parameters will be recovered.
Raw answers are scored and screened for miskeys, straight-lining and rapid guessing before any model is fitted.

The calibration with mirt is checked from convergence to item fit, local dependence, DIF, reliability and person fit, and the calibrated items are stored in an item bank and linked to its scale through anchor items.
Build and decide.
Parallel forms are assembled to the blueprint, and adaptive and multistage tests are simulated from the bank.
Cut scores come with their classification accuracy and consistency.
Open-ended responses are scored by a rubric-based language model or a trained engine, and machine scores are used only after they agree with human scores, overall and within groups.
Operate.
Security checks look for preknowledge, leaked items, answer copying and aberrant response times.
A technical report lists every stage, every flag and every decision, with the code that reproduces them, and bank monitoring shows where the bank is thin, which starts the next round of item writing.
Each stage ends with a gate.
Every check compares a statistic with a threshold from mv_rules(), which follow common operational practice and can each be changed by name.
A flag is information, a matter for review, or a block that makes later stages unsafe.
The analyst can acknowledge or override a flag, or drop an item, and each decision is recorded with its reason.
In strict mode, a stage will not start while an earlier stage has open review or block flags, so no problem is passed over without a recorded decision.
The Pipeline tab of the workbench shows the same stages and flags without code.
The pipeline is where the two halves of mirtverse meet.

The AI functions are not a separate toolbox: Generated items enter at the same gates as written ones, machine scores must pass agreement checks against human scores before they count, and ai_audit() and validity_argument() feed the same technical report as the calibration.
A worked example on the package website takes a simulated certification exam through every stage, with problems planted in the data for the gates to find.
Because many users meet IRT in a course, mirtverse ships with material for teaching it.

An open textbook (Bulut, 2026a) covers measurement, IRT models, estimation, dimensionality, fit, information, scoring, polytomous models, DIF, linking, item banks and adaptive testing, reporting, and a part on AI in measurement, with every example run in mirt and mirtverse.
Ten interactive labs (run_lab()) use datasets with planted features, such as a miskeyed item or a DIF item, so students practise finding problems rather than reading about them.
An instructor toolkit creates new courses and labs, swaps lab datasets and checks material before class, and a Model Context Protocol server exposes the toolkit to AI assistants.

A sample syllabus, a case study with a full technical report, a workshop kit on AI in measurement, short narrated video demonstrations, and a "thesis kit" that walks graduate students from item responses to a Methods section complete the set.
mirtverse was first released in October 2026 (version 0.1.0) and reached version 0.2.0 later that month, archived on Zenodo (Bulut, 2026b).

text.text: The package targets graduate courses in educational and psychological measurement, testing and credentialing programs that need reproducible operational analyses, and researchers who want to study AI methods in measurement with transparent, checkable tools.

Its near-term significance lies in three areas: Lowering the entry cost of rigorous IRT analysis for students and non-R users, making AI-assisted item development and scoring auditable within an open psychometric workflow, and giving instructors ready-made, reproducible teaching material built on the same software their students will use in practice.
Generative AI was used extensively in this project.

Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, drafted most of the R code, tests and documentation, the companion textbook chapters and teaching labs, and a first draft of this paper, working in the project's version-controlled repository under the author's direction.
The author defined the scope, made the design and methodological decisions, chose the defaults and thresholds, and reviewed each change before it was merged through a pull request.

Correctness was checked in several ways: An automated test suite with more than 200 tests; R CMD check on Linux, macOS and Windows for every change through continuous integration; comparisons with established implementations (mirt itself for all estimates, LNIRT for the response-time model, cacIRT for classification accuracy and consistency); and teaching datasets with known, planted properties that the functions must recover.
All references in this paper were checked against their published sources by the author.

The mirtverse workflow: Bring your data, fit and choose a model, understand the results, and share them.
Tidy results and graphics. tidy(), glance() and augment() methods return item parameters, model fit and person scores as data frames.

The gg_*() functions draw trace lines, information and standard error curves, Wright maps, item fit, 𝑄 3 local dependence heat maps, DIF and score distributions as ggplot2 objects that users can restyle.
